source_text: Proinde sciit, et quando pati oporteret eum, cuius passionem lex figura(ra)t. nam ex tot festis Iudaeorum paschae diem elegit in hoc enim sacramentum pronuntiarat Moyses: pascha est domini. ideo et adfectum suum ostendit: concupiscentia concupii pascha edere uobiscum, antequam patiar. o legis destructorem, qui concupierat etiam pascha seruare! nimirum uerbecina illum [in] Iudaica delectarat. an ipse erat, qui, tamquam ouis ad uictimam adduci habens et tamquam ouis coram tondente sic os non aperturus, figuram sanguinis sui salutaris implere concupiscebat? poterat et ab extraneo quolibet tradi, ne dicerem et in hoc psalmum expunctum: qui mecum panem edit leuauit in me plantam. poterat et sine praemio tradi. quanta enim opera traditoris circa eum, qui populum coram offendens nec tradi magis potuisset quam inuadi? sed hoc alii competisset Christo, non qui prophetias adimplebat. scriptum est enim: pro eo quod uenumdederunt iustum. nam et quantitatem et exitum pretii postea Iuda paenitente reuocati et in emptionem dati agri figuli, sicut in euangelio Mathei continetur, Hieremias praecanit: et acceperunt triginta argentea pretium adpretiati — uel honorati - et dederunt ea in agrum figuli. professus itaque se concupiscentia concupisse edere pascha ut suum, — indignum enim, ut quid alienum concupisceret deus — acceptum panem et distributum discipulis corpus suum illum fecit hoc est corpus meum dicendo, id est (figura. corporis mei\'. figura autem non fuisset nisi ueritatis esset corpus. ceterum uacua res, quod est phantasma, figuram capere non posset. aut si propterea panem corpus sibi finxit, quia corporis carebat uanitatem, ergo panem debuit tradere pro nobis. faciebat ad uanitatem Marcionis, ut panis crucifigeretur. cur autem panem corpus suum appellat et non magis peponem, quem Marcion cordis loco habuit, non intellegens ueterem fuisse istam figuram corporis Christi dicentis per Hieremiam: aduersus me cogitauerunt cogitatum dicentes: uenite. coiciamus lignum in panem eius, scilicet crucem in corpus eius? itaque inluminator antiquitatum, quid tunc uoluerit significasse panem, satis declarauit corpus suum uocans panemsic et in calicis mentione testamentum constituens sanguine suo obsignatum substantiam corporis confirmauit. nullius enim corporis sanguis potest esse nisi carnis. nam et si qua corporis qualitas non carnea opponetur nobis, certe sanguinem nisi carnea non habebit. ita consistet probatio corporis de testimonio carnis, probatio carnis de testimonio sanguinis. ut autem et sanguinis ueterem figuram in uino recognoseas. aderit Esaias: quis, inquit, qui aduenit ex Edom, rubor uestimentorum eius ex Bosor? sic decorus in stola uiolentia cum fortitudine? quare rubra uestimenta tua, et indumenta sicut de foro torcularis, pleno conculcato? spiritus enim propheticus, uelut iam contemplabundus dominum ad passionem uenientem, carne scilicet uestitum ut in ea passum, cruentum habitum carnis in uestimentorum rubore designat, conculcatae et expressae ui passionis tamquam in foro torcularis, quia et inde quasi cruentati homines de uini rubore descendunt. multo manifestius Genesis in benedictione Iudae, ex cuius tribu carnis census Christi processurus, iam tunc Christum in Iuda deliniabat: lauabit, inquit, in uino stolam suam et in sanguine uuae amictum suum, stolam et amictum carnem demonstrans et uinum sanguinem. ita et nunc sanguinem suum in uino consecrauit qui tunc uinum in sanguinem figurauit.
thought_title: Christ's Passion and the Lord's Supper
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, He knew, and when it was necessary for Him to suffer, whose passion the law had prefigured. For from all the festivals of the Jews, He chose the day of the Passover, for in this, Moses had pronounced the sacrament: the Passover is of the Lord. Therefore, He also showed His affection: I have earnestly desired to eat the Passover with you before I suffer. O destroyer of the law, who also desired to keep the Passover! Doubtless, the verdant things of Judaism had delighted Him. Or was He Himself, who, like a sheep being led to sacrifice and like a sheep before the shearer, would not open His mouth, desiring to fulfill the figure of His salutary blood? He could have been betrayed by any stranger, so that I would not say that even this psalm was fulfilled: he who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me. He could have been betrayed without a reward. For how great were the works of the betrayer around Him, who, offending the people before Him, could not have been betrayed more than He was invaded? But this would have been fitting for another, not for Christ, who fulfilled the prophecies. For it is written: because they sold the just one. For also, the quantity and outcome of the price, afterwards, when Judas repented and the pieces of silver were returned and given for the purchase of the potter's field, as is contained in the Gospel of Matthew, Jeremiah had prophesied: and they took thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one who was valued - or honored - and they gave them for the potter's field. Therefore, having professed that He had desired to eat the Passover with His own, - for it was not fitting that God should desire something alien - having taken bread and distributed it to the disciples, He made His body, saying, this is my body, that is, the figure of my body. But the figure would not have been unless the body was of truth. Moreover, an empty thing, which is a phantom, could not take on a figure. Or if, for this reason, He made bread His body, because He lacked a body, then He ought to have given bread for us. He was making a mockery of Marcion's vanity, so that bread might be crucified. But why does He call bread His body and not rather a gourd, which Marcion had in the place of a heart, not understanding that this was an old figure of the body of Christ, who spoke through Jeremiah: they have thought against me, saying, come, let us cast wood into his bread, that is, the cross into his body? Therefore, the illuminator of ancient things has sufficiently declared what He then wished to signify by bread, calling His body bread, and in the mention of the cup, establishing the testament confirmed by His blood, He confirmed the substance of the body. For the blood of no body can be except of flesh. For even if some quality of the body is opposed to us as not fleshly, certainly it will not have blood except as fleshly. So the proof of the body consists in the testimony of the flesh, the proof of the flesh in the testimony of the blood. But so that you may also recognize the old figure of the blood in wine, Isaiah will be present: who, he says, is this who comes from Edom, the redness of whose garments is from Bozrah? So becoming in a robe of violence with strength? Why are your garments red, and your clothes like those from the wine press, fully trodden? For the prophetic spirit, as if already contemplating the Lord coming to His passion, clothed in flesh, so that He suffered in it, designates the bloody habit of the flesh in the redness of the garments, trodden and pressed by the force of the passion, as if in a wine press, because from there, men, as if made bloody, descend from the redness of the wine. Much more clearly, in the blessing of Judah, in Genesis, from whose tribe the census of the flesh of Christ was to come, He was already then outlining Christ in Judah: He will wash, he says, His robe in wine and His garment in the blood of the grape, demonstrating the flesh by the robe and the garment, and the wine by the blood. So also now, He consecrated His blood in wine, who then prefigured wine in blood.

pass_b_english: He knew exactly what He was doing, and He knew precisely when He had to suffer, since the Law had already sketched out His passion in advance. Out of every Jewish festival, He picked the Passover, because Moses had already declared the mystery: the Passover belongs to the Lord. That is why He let His desire show: 'I have earnestly wanted to eat this Passover with you before I suffer' (Luke 22:15). Oh, you destroyer of the Law, who still wanted to keep the Passover! No doubt the fresh green rites of Judaism had charmed Him. Or was it that He Himself — led like a sheep to slaughter, silent like a sheep before its shearer — was aching to fulfill the figure of His saving blood (Isaiah 53:7)? He could have been handed over by any random stranger, so I would not even have to say this psalm was fulfilled: 'The one who eats my bread has lifted his heel against me' (Psalm 41:9). He could have been betrayed for nothing. After all, what great effort did the betrayer expend on a man who, by offending the people to their faces, could not have been seized more easily than invaded? But that scenario would have suited some other Christ, not the One who actually fulfilled the prophecies. Scripture says: 'Because they sold the Righteous One' (Zechariah 11:12-13). And the exact amount and final disposition of the price — later, when Judas repented and the silver was returned and used to buy the potter's field, as Matthew's Gospel records (Matthew 27:3-10) — Jeremiah had already foretold: 'They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the One they valued — or honored — and gave them for the potter's field' (Jeremiah 32:9).

So, having confessed that He had longed to eat the Passover with His own — for it would have been unfitting for God to long for something alien — He took bread, distributed it to the disciples, and made it His body by saying, 'This is My body,' that is, the figure of My body (Luke 22:19). But a figure cannot exist unless the reality exists. A phantom, an empty thing, cannot take on a figure. Or if He called bread His body because He lacked a body, then He should have given bread for us — making a mockery of Marcion's fantasy, so that bread might be crucified. But why call bread His body and not a gourd, which Marcion kept in place of a heart? He fails to grasp that this was an ancient figure of Christ's body, spoken through Jeremiah: 'They plotted against me, saying, Come, let us put wood into his bread' — that is, the cross into His body (Jeremiah 11:19). Therefore the Illuminator of ancient things has made it perfectly clear what He meant by bread: by calling His body bread, and by establishing the covenant in the cup, sealed with His blood, He confirmed the substance of the body (Luke 22:20). No body can have blood except a fleshly one. Even if someone posits a non-fleshly quality of body, it still would not have blood except as flesh. So the proof of the body rests on the testimony of the flesh, and the proof of the flesh rests on the testimony of the blood.

And so that you may also recognize the ancient figure of blood in wine, Isaiah steps forward: 'Who is this coming from Edom, with crimsoned garments from Bozrah? Who is this, glorious in His apparel, marching in the greatness of His strength? Why are Your garments red, and Your clothes like one who treads in the winepress?' (Isaiah 63:1-3). The prophetic Spirit, as if already gazing on the Lord coming to His passion, clothed in flesh so that He might suffer in it, marks the blood-stained condition of the flesh by the redness of the garments — trampled and pressed by the violence of the passion, as in a winepress, because from there men descend as if bloodied by the redness of wine. Even more plainly, Genesis in the blessing of Judah — from whose tribe the lineage of Christ's flesh would arise — was already sketching Christ in Judah: 'He will wash His robe in wine and His garment in the blood of the grape' (Genesis 49:11), identifying the robe and garment as flesh, and the wine as blood. So now He has consecrated His blood in wine, He who then prefigured wine as blood.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the reality of Christ's flesh versus Marcionite docetism. All scripture citations in Pass B (Luke 22:15, Isaiah 53:7, Psalm 41:9, Zechariah 11:12-13, Matthew 27:3-10, Jeremiah 32:9, Luke 22:19, Jeremiah 11:19, Luke 22:20, Isaiah 63:1-3, Genesis 49:11) are correctly identified based on the Latin text's allusions and content, fulfilling the requirement to add identifications. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Locked Latin.
